title: Writing on Skin
description: A fingertip moving in deliberate patterns on skin produces a specific quality of attention — on the writer's side and the receiver's. Add guessing what's being written and you get something sensation and communication can't quite do separately.
equipment: Just yourselves. Optionally: a blunt stylus or the capped end of a pen for variety.

instructions.label: Solo first
instructions.content: Trace letters slowly on your own inner forearm using a single fingertip — light enough that the contact is precise. Notice whether you can feel each letter as sensation separate from your knowledge of what you're writing. This is calibration: you're checking how much information your skin actually carries, and whether very slow, deliberate contact there produces any response worth building on.

instructions.label: With a partner (the real version)
instructions.content: Receiver lies still with eyes closed. Giver traces single letters, then short words, on the receiver's back, shoulder, or inner arm — slowly enough that each stroke is distinct. The receiver guesses what's being written; getting it wrong means the giver continues with the same word until they get it. Move through a few words, then switch roles. The guessing dimension isn't incidental: it keeps the receiver's attention entirely on the sensation, and it gives the giver a reason to be deliberate and slow. What you choose to write is up to you.

explore: Solo: can you actually feel what you're writing on yourself, or does your knowledge of the letter override the sensation?
As receiver: which areas produce clearer sensation — back, arm, stomach, inner thigh?
Does getting a letter wrong — and having it retraced — change how it registers the second time?
As giver: does choosing what to write, and writing it slowly enough to be felt, produce any quality of its own?
why: The skin reads pressure, direction, and sequence rather than meaning — but the brain tries to make meaning from it anyway, which creates unusual attentional focus in both people. The receiver is trying to decode sensation; the giver is trying to produce it precisely. This split is different from most forms of touch, which tend toward either sensation or communication rather than both at once. The guessing mechanic keeps the receiver present in a way that simple tracing doesn't require, and the giver necessarily slows down to a pace the skin can actually read.
